title: The lambda (SOS2-style) formulation built from binaries

blocks.text: 6.6.2 The Lambda (SOS2-Style) Formulation Built From Binaries

Lesson 6.6.1 ended with the treasury's second offer for the small portfolio: a credit line whose first $1,500k costs 0.45 per $k drawn, the next $1,500k 0.25 and the last $2,000k 0.10. The cost is concave, the objective pushes it down, and the segment rows let the solver take the cheap tiers first: the model charged $620k for a draw that really costs $1,110k. The planners still want the true best plan under this offer. That needs a formulation that is exact for a curve of any shape, pushed either way. This lesson builds the standard one, the lambda form, from MathOpt's plain binary variables, in four rules.
GridCap is a fictional utility's portfolio, generated for this course; the credit line and the board approval are invented.
Weights on the Breakpoints Describe Every Point of the Curve

Take the curve's breakpoints $`(X_0, F_0), \dots, (X_K, F_K)`$; for the falling tiers they are (0, 0), (1,500, 675), (3,000, 1,050) and (5,000, 1,250). Give each breakpoint a weight $`\lambda_j \ge 0`$, the weights adding up to 1, and let the point be the weighted average of the breakpoints:
b = \sum_{j=0}^{K} \lambda_j X_j, \qquad y = \sum_{j=0}^{K} \lambda_j F_j, \qquad \sum_{j=0}^{K} \lambda_j = 1, \qquad \lambda_j \ge 0

A weighted average of points with non-negative weights that add up to 1 is a **convex combination** of them (lesson 1.2.3). Every point of the curve is one. A draw of $2,000k lies on the segment from 1,500 to 3,000, a third of the way along, so $`\lambda_1 = 2/3`$, $`\lambda_2 = 1/3`$ and the others 0 give $`b = 2{,}000`$ and $`y = \tfrac23 \cdot 675 + \tfrac13 \cdot 1{,}050 = 800`$, the true cost.

The trouble is the converse. The weights describe every convex combination of the breakpoints, not only the points on the curve. $`\lambda_0 = 0.6`$ and $`\lambda_3 = 0.4`$ also give $`b = 2{,}000`$, with $`y = 0.4 \times 1{,}250 = 500`$: a point on the straight line from the first breakpoint to the last, below the curve. The program fixes $`b`$ and asks HiGHS for the lowest and highest $`y`$ the weights allow:

MathOpt Model methods naming SOS: []
CP-SAT CpModel methods naming SOS: []
falling tiers, breakpoints [(0.0, 0.0), (1500.0, 675.0), (3000.0, 1050.0), (5000.0, 1250.0)]
x     | f(x) | weights only  | weights + segment binaries
1000  |  450 | 250 to 450    | 450
2000  |  800 | 500 to 800    | 800
3500  | 1100 | 875 to 1100   | 1100
4500  | 1200 | 1125 to 1200  | 1200

(The first two lines and the last column belong to the next two rules.) With weights only, $`y`$ may lie anywhere between the chord from the first to the last breakpoint and the curve itself. A cost pushed down slides to the chord. On GridCap small the program solves the credit-line model of lesson 6.6.1 with the cost written as weights only:

weights only          : objective $26,768k, drawn $4,900k, weights [0.02, 0.0, 0.0, 0.98]
                        cost charged $1,225k, real cost $1,240k, plan really worth $26,753k

The solver put its weight on breakpoints 0 and 3, which are not neighbours, and charged $1,225k for a $4,900k draw that really costs $1,240k. Here the plan happens to be right and the claim is off by $15k; at other draws the table shows the gap reaching $300k (at $2,000k: 500 against 800).
Two Neighbouring Weights Pin the Point to the Curve

The fix is a rule about which weights may be positive: **at most two, and they must be neighbours**, $`\lambda_{k-1}`$ and $`\lambda_k`$ for one segment $`k`$. A convex combination of two neighbouring breakpoints is a point on the straight piece between them, which is the curve. So with the rule, every allowed $`(b, y)`$ is on the curve, and every point of the curve is allowed. The rule does not care about the curve's shape or the push, which is what this lesson needed.

An ordered list of variables of which at most two may be nonzero, and only two consecutive ones, is called a **special ordered set of type 2**, or **SOS2**; Vielma's survey traces SOS constraints to Beale and Tomlin. (Type 1, SOS1, allows at most one nonzero.) Some modeling tools hand an SOS2 constraint to the solver as it is (Pyomo's `Piecewise` does by default, lesson 6.6.4). MathOpt's Python model cannot: the first line of the output above lists every method of `mathopt.Model` whose name mentions SOS, and the second every such method of CP-SAT's `CpModel`; there is none. The OR-Tools MathOpt overview lists SOS among the constraint kinds MathOpt's design covers, but OR-Tools 9.15's Python `Model` (`model.py`) has `add_linear_constraint`, `add_quadratic_constraint` and `add_indicator_constraint` and no SOS method. So in this course the rule is written with binaries, which every MILP solver accepts.
One Binary per Segment Enforces the Neighbour Rule

Give each segment $`k = 1, \dots, K`$ a binary $`z_k`$: 1 if the point lies on segment $`k`$. Exactly one segment is chosen, and a breakpoint may carry weight only if a segment it belongs to is chosen. Breakpoint 0 belongs to segment 1 only, breakpoint $`K`$ to segment $`K`$ only, and every other breakpoint $`j`$ to segments $`j`$ and $`j+1`$:

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^{K} z_k &= 1 && \text{(one segment)} \\
\lambda_0 &\le z_1 && \\
\lambda_j &\le z_j + z_{j+1} && j = 1, \dots, K-1 \quad \text{(near}_j) \\
\lambda_K &\le z_K && \\
z_k &\in \{0, 1\} && k = 1, \dots, K
\end{aligned}

Read it for one choice: $`z_2 = 1`$ and the others 0. Then $`\lambda_0 \le 0`$, $`\lambda_1 \le 1`$, $`\lambda_2 \le 1`$, $`\lambda_3 \le 0`$: only the two ends of segment 2 may carry weight, and the point lies on segment 2. Each choice of $`z`$ opens exactly one segment, and the weights must add up to 1 on it. This is the standard MIP formulation of SOS2 in Vielma's survey (section 6), the constraint written with binaries instead of being handed to the solver:

n = len(curve.xs)
lam = [model.add_variable(lb=0, ub=1, name=f"{name}_lam{j}") for j in range(n)]
model.add_linear_constraint(sum(lam) == 1, name=f"{name}_weights")
seg = []
if binaries:
    seg = [model.add_binary_variable(name=f"{name}_seg{k}") for k in range(n - 1)]
    model.add_linear_constraint(sum(seg) == 1, name=f"{name}_one_segment")
    for j in range(n):
        touching = [seg[k] for k in (j - 1, j) if 0 <= k < n - 1]
        model.add_linear_constraint(lam[j] <= sum(touching), name=f"{name}_near{j}")
x = sum(curve.xs[j] * lam[j] for j in range(n))
y = sum(curve.ys[j] * lam[j] for j in range(n))

(Python numbers segments from 0, so `seg[k]` is $`z_{k+1}`$ and breakpoint `j` touches `seg[j-1]` and `seg[j]`.) The last column of the table above is this form: at every fixed draw, the lowest and the highest $`y`$ coincide, and they are $`f(b)`$. On GridCap small:

weights + seg binaries: objective $26,753k, drawn $4,900k, weights [0.0, 0.0, 0.05, 0.95]
                        cost charged $1,240k, real cost $1,240k, plan really worth $26,753k
                        segment binaries [0, 0, 1]

The solver chose segment 3, put its weight on breakpoints 2 and 3 (5% and 95%: a draw of $`0.05 \times 3{,}000 + 0.95 \times 5{,}000 = 4{,}900`$), and charged the real cost. The objective, $26,753k, is now what the plan is really worth, and it is the true best plan under the falling-tier offer. Compare lesson 6.6.1: the segment rows chose a $3,600k draw and claimed $26,861k for a plan worth $26,371k.
The price is $`K`$ binaries per curve, here 3, on top of the 40 project binaries. Lesson 6.6.3 shows two other ways to write the same rule, one with fewer binaries.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Segment Binaries Are Decisions Other Rules Can Use

$`z_k`$ is not only bookkeeping: it says which segment the plan is on, and other rules can read it. GridCap's board must approve any draw from the last tier, above $3,000k, and an approval costs the treasury $`A`$ thousand dollars in fees and time. One binary $`a`$ for the approval, and one row:
a \ge z_3 \qquad \text{(needs\_board)}, \qquad \text{objective} \;-\; A\,a

board = sel.model.add_binary_variable(name="board")
sel.model.add_linear_constraint(board >= loan.binaries[2], name="needs_board")
sel.model.maximize(sel.model.objective.as_linear_expression() - approval * board)

the board must approve any draw from the last tier (above $3,000k); approval costs $A k
  A = 200: objective $26,553k, drawn $4,900k, segment binaries [0, 0, 1], board 1
  A = 500: objective $26,253k, drawn $4,900k, segment binaries [0, 0, 1], board 1
  A = 800: objective $26,043k, drawn $2,970k, segment binaries [0, 1, 0], board 0
Up to $500k of approval cost, the large draw still pays. At $800k, the plan stays in segment 2, draws $2,970k and skips the board.

One detail decides how such a rule reads: **at a breakpoint, both neighbouring segments are allowed.** A draw of exactly $3,000k is the end of segment 2 and the start of segment 3; with $`z_2 = 1`$ it is $`\lambda_2 = 1`$, and no approval is triggered. So $`a \ge z_3`$ states "a draw *above* $3,000k needs the board", which is what the board asked for. A rule that must fire *at* $3,000k as well cannot be written with $`z`$ alone: the model can always place a draw of exactly $3,000k on segment 2. A MILP cannot tell "above" from "at least" on a continuous quantity, so when the difference matters, ask the business which side the threshold belongs to and put the breakpoint there.
<!-- practice 2 -->
The Model
The selection model of lesson 1.1.1 on GridCap small with the falling-tier credit line in lambda form, marked. `credit_exact.py` solves it, then adds the board approval of the last rule.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the candidate projects; $`M`$, $`C`$ and $`\mathcal{G}`$ the must-do projects, the child projects (parent $`p(c)`$) and the alternative groups; $`j = 0, \dots, K`$ the credit line's breakpoints and $`k = 1, \dots, K`$ its segments ($`K = 3`$). ← this lesson

**Parameters.** $`\text{capex}_i`$ and $`\text{npv}_i`$ ($k); $`B = 38{,}390`$ ($k); $`(X_j, F_j)`$, the breakpoints: $k drawn and its total cost, (0, 0), (1,500, 675), (3,000, 1,050), (5,000, 1,250); $`A`$, the board's approval cost ($k), in the last rule only. ← this lesson
**Variables.**
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \text{npv}_i\, x_i - \sum_{j=0}^{K} F_j\, \lambda_j \;\big[\, - A\, a \,\big]
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i \in P} \text{capex}_i\, x_i &\le B + \sum_{j=0}^{K} X_j\, \lambda_j && && \text{(budget)} \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
\sum_{j=0}^{K} \lambda_j &= 1 && && \text{(loan\_weights)} \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
\sum_{k=1}^{K} z_k &= 1 && && \text{(loan\_one\_segment)} \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
\lambda_j &\le z_j + z_{j+1} && j = 0, \dots, K \quad (z_0 = z_{K+1} = 0) && \text{(loan\_near}_j) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
a &\ge z_K && && \text{(needs\_board; last rule only)} \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
x_i &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
x_c &\le x_{p(c)} && \forall c \in C && \text{(parent}_c) \\
\sum_{i \in g} x_i &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g)
\end{aligned}
In the code the segments are `loan_seg0` to `loan_seg2` and the near rows `loan_near0` to `loan_near3`.
Summary

items: **Weights on the breakpoints describe every point of the curve.** But weights alone allow any convex combination of breakpoints, so a cost pushed down slides to the chord below the curve.
**Two neighbouring weights pin the point to the curve.** The rule is SOS2; MathOpt's Python model (OR-Tools 9.15) has no SOS method, so it is written with binaries.
**One binary per segment enforces the neighbour rule.** $`\sum_k z_k = 1`$ and $`\lambda_j \le z_j + z_{j+1}`$; exact for any shape and any push. GridCap's falling tiers: $26,753k, the true best.
**The segment binaries are decisions other rules can use.** $`a \ge z_3`$ charges the board's approval exactly when the draw is above $3,000k; at a breakpoint either segment is allowed.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: a weighted average with non-negative weights adding up to 1 (lesson 1.2.3)
an ordered set of variables with at most one nonzero / at most two, consecutive
a curve written as weights on its breakpoints (also called the convex combination model)

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (the model features MathOpt lists, SOS constraints among them, and the solvers it calls); [MathOpt `Model` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/model.py) (its `add_*` methods, none of them for SOS in the Python API); [CP-SAT `cp_model` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/sat/python/cp_model.py) (CP-SAT's `CpModel` methods, none of them for SOS either); [Vielma, Mixed Integer Linear Programming Formulation Techniques](https://juan-pablo-vielma.github.io/publications/Mixed-Integer-Linear-Programming-Formulation-Techniques.pdf) (section 6, Example 10: SOS1, SOS2 and their standard binary formulations); [Integer Programming, Chapter 9 of Applied Mathematical Programming (MIT 15.053)](https://web.mit.edu/15.053/www/AMP-Chapter-09.pdf) (section 9.2: economies of scale in a maximization need the binary formulation).
Challenges

items: Write the rows for a curve with a single segment ($`K = 1`$). How many binaries does it need, and why?
Change `needs_board` so the board must approve any draw of $3,000k or more. What does the model do at exactly $3,000k now? (Hint: add a tiny gap, or a fourth breakpoint.)
Use the lambda form for the *rising* tiers of lesson 6.6.1. The plan cannot change; does anything in the model's size or LP bound?

blocks.text: Design Note: One Formulation per Curve, Chosen by Its Shape

The lambda form is always correct, so it is tempting to use it for every curve. It costs a binary per segment, and lesson 6.6.1 showed that a convex cost pushed down, or a concave value pushed up, needs none. A model builder that checks each curve's shape and push, and writes the binary-free form when it is enough, keeps the search over the project decisions only. The renewal model of lesson 6.6.4 does this per asset. Keep the check and the choice in one function, so a reviewer sees in one place why a curve did or did not get binaries.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**adjacent_weights.py.** Checks MathOpt for an SOS method, then fixes the draw and asks how low and high the cost may go with weights only and with segment binaries (*Weights on the Breakpoints*, *One Binary per Segment*). *Try:* Add 3000 to `POINTS`. Predict both columns at that draw.

**credit_exact.py.** Solves GridCap small with the falling tiers as weights only and with segment binaries, then adds the board approval (*Weights on the Breakpoints*, *One Binary per Segment*, *The Segment Binaries Are Decisions*). *Try:* Set the approval cost to 650. Predict whether the plan crosses into the last tier.
**piecewise.py.** The curve and the formulations; `add_lambda` is this lesson's.

**credit_line.py.** Lesson 6.6.1's program: the two credit lines and `with_credit`, which puts any formulation of a curve into the selection model. *Try:* Solve the falling tiers with `add_lambda` in place of `add_segments`. Predict the objective.
